📚 Today you learned

Order Fill Confirmation — "Should Have Triggered" Isn't the Same as "Did"

A stop order firing is an event in your broker's system, not a fact you can derive from price alone. SPXC's plain STOP sits at $186.90; an unverified snapshot has the stock at $174.65, comfortably through it. Logically the stop should have executed days ago — but "price crossed the trigger" and "the broker's matching engine actually routed and filled the order" are two different claims, and only IBKR's order/trade log can confirm the second one. Gaps, brief trading halts, and even data errors in third-party snapshots can all produce a "should have filled" that turns out wrong. The rule: treat any stop as unconfirmed until you've seen the fill (or the order still resting) in the broker itself — never assume execution from a price chart, especially on a name you're already watching closely for other reasons.

Also today: Trading halt — exchanges can pause a stock mid-session on volatility or news; a resting stop can't fill during a halt no matter how far price has moved once trading resumes.
